title: What should you do yourself?
principle: Own your core skill. Pay others for the rest.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a big decision. In 2004, Bharti Airtel had about 58 lakh mobile customers and was growing fast. Then it asked Ericsson and Nokia to run its network, the towers and machines that carry calls, and IBM to run its computers. Can you guess why?

screens.prompt: Why would a phone company pay other companies to run its mobile network?

options.label: Its own network kept breaking down
The government asked it to do this
It wanted more time to win customers

screens.why: Airtel paid only for the network capacity its calls used, not to own the network. That left more time and money to win customers. By July 2006, it had more than 2.4 crore mobile customers.

screens.title: Your core skill
screens.text: Airtel kept the job it saw as most important: winning and keeping customers. In 1990, two professors named this idea core competence: a skill that makes customers choose you and is hard to copy. Keep that skill, and pay others for work they can do better or cheaper.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: A phone company and a home bakery both have something customers choose them for. It's September, your fifth year. Your ₹850 chocolate cake costs ₹400 to make. You, your sister and your cousin bake, but you also make 120 deliveries a month, print boxes and file GST yourselves.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six jobs at your bakery. For each one, tell me: should you do it yourselves, or pay someone else?

items.text: Mixing cakes from your own recipe
Tasting every cake before it leaves

screens.why: Exactly. Airtel's core was its customers. Yours is making cakes people love: your recipe, your checks and your regular customers are why you can sell cakes for ₹850. Delivery, printing and GST matter too, and you're still responsible for them, but a rider, a printer or a CA can do them well, often for less.

screens.prompt: You make 120 deliveries a month. Your own rider costs ₹12,000 a month. A delivery service charges ₹60 per trip. Which is cheaper?
screens.why: Right. 120 trips × ₹60 is ₹7,200, so the service costs ₹4,800 less than your own rider each month. And you pay only for the trips you make.

wrong.b: Your own rider costs ₹12,000 whatever happens. The service is 120 × ₹60 = ₹7,200. That's ₹4,800 less each month.
wrong.c: Let's check. 120 × ₹60 = ₹7,200. Your rider costs ₹12,000. That's a gap of ₹4,800 a month.

screens.prompt: Your own rider costs ₹12,000 a month. A delivery service charges ₹60 per trip. At how many trips will both cost the same?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹12,000 ÷ ₹60 = 200 trips. Below 200 trips, the service costs less. And your rider costs ₹12,000 even in a slow month: at 60 trips, the service costs ₹3,600.

wrong.a: That's how many trips you make now. To find where they cost the same, divide ₹12,000 by ₹60. That's 200 trips.
wrong.c: Let's check: 300 trips × ₹60 = ₹18,000, more than the rider's ₹12,000. Divide instead: ₹12,000 ÷ ₹60 = 200 trips.

screens.prompt: Your cake costs ₹400 to make. A factory that bakes for 50 shops offers you cakes from its own recipe at ₹300. Biggest risk?

options.label: No risk, you save ₹100 per cake
The factory might deliver cakes late
Your cake tastes like other shops' cakes

screens.why: Exactly. Your cake's taste is your core. Customers pay ₹850 because they like your cake. If you buy factory cakes, other shops can sell the same ones, and customers have less reason to choose you.

wrong.a: You'd save ₹100 a cake. But customers pay ₹850 for your taste. Use a factory's recipe, and any shop can sell the same cake. Your taste is what you must keep.
wrong.c: Late cakes are a problem you could fix. The bigger risk is that your taste, the reason people pay ₹850, would no longer be yours.

screens.setup: It's late September. You expect about 200 orders in October, up from 120. The three of you can bake that many cakes, but not also deliver 200 orders yourselves. Each cake sells for ₹850.
screens.question: How do you get ready for Diwali?

options.label: Buy factory cakes for the extra Diwali orders
options.outcome: You finish every Diwali order. But some regular customers get factory cakes, notice the different taste, and talk about it in the colony group. In November, your orders fall below 120.
options.why: You gave away the one thing customers came for. Your taste is your core, so it's the last thing to give away.
options.better: Keep the baking. Pay others for delivery and printing.

options.label: Hire your own rider; he's there every day
options.outcome: Diwali deliveries go well. You pay ₹12,000 a month for the rider and ₹2,500 a month for his scooter loan. In November, deliveries fall to about 90. A delivery service would cost ₹5,400, but your rider still costs ₹12,000.
options.why: Deliveries worked, but you took on a fixed cost for a busy month. Delivery isn't your core, so there was no need to own it.
options.better: Pay a delivery service per trip, and keep the baking yourselves.

options.label: Pay a delivery service per trip; you bake
options.outcome: In October, the service makes 200 deliveries for ₹12,000, the same as your own rider. In November, it makes about 90 for ₹5,400, saving you ₹6,600. You spend Diwali baking, and your regular customers keep ordering.
options.why: Exactly. You kept your core, the baking, and paid others only for what you used. When the rush ended, the cost fell with it.

screens.text: Your ___ is your cake's taste, so you bake the cakes. You pay a CA to file your ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Keep the skill that makes customers choose you. Pay others for jobs they can do as well, or better. That's core competence.

summary: Core competence: the skill that makes customers choose you, and that others find hard to copy.
Own your core. Pay others for the rest, and pay only for what you use.
Never give away your core, even when it's cheaper.

cards.front: Your tailoring shop is known for perfect fitting. What should you never give to others?
cards.back: That's your core competence. Own it. Pay others for the rest.

cards.front: Own rider: ₹10,000 a month. Service: ₹50 a trip. You make 100 trips. Which costs less?
cards.back: 100 × ₹50 = ₹5,000. Delivery isn't your core, so pay per trip.

cards.front: A factory offers to make your best seller for less. What's the risk?
cards.back: Give away your core, and customers lose their reason to choose you.
